papers.title_in_file: Controlling Search in Very Large Commonsense Knowledge Bases: A Machine Learning Approach
papers.what_it_is: A Cycorp paper that proposes two learned node-ordering heuristics (restriction-condition decision trees and a linear regression on search-state features) for backward inference in the Cyc knowledge base and reports their speedup on thousands of Cyc queries.

assertions.value: The authors report that experimental results over thousands of queries show an order of magnitude speedup from the two heuristics.
quotes: Experimental results over thousands of queries
show an order of magnitude speedup.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one knowledge base.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 3 (read from the jumbled text layer) gives DT+SL speedups of about 16.6, 13.5 and 14.7 for the three test sets, and a Q/A improvement column; the cutoff of 5 minutes per query bounds the baseline times.

assertions.value: The authors report that the average speedup over the baseline is a factor of 14, and that decision trees and multiple-regression models each led to significant speedups.
quotes: We see that both decision trees and multiple regression based models have led to significant speedups.
The average speedup is a factor of 14.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The per-set DT+SL speedups in Table 3 are 16.61, 13.50 and 14.69, whose mean is about 14.9; the text's figure of 14 appears to be rounded down or computed another way.

assertions.value: The authors state that because the heuristics steer the inference engine toward more productive parts of the search space, question-answering performance improves too, measured relative to the baseline in the column labeled Q/A Imp. (%).
quotes: they improve question-answering (Q/A) performance too.
shows the improvement in Q/A performance with respect to the baseline.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: In Table 3 the share of queries answered rises from 48, 64 and 26 percent (baseline, test sets 1 to 3) to 99, 96 and 92 percent with DT+SL; this is read from the jumbled table layout.

assertions.value: The authors divided the benchmark queries by their terms into three test sets (military and asymmetrical warfare, biology, and others such as commonsense queries) and restricted the cutoff time of each query to 5 minutes.
quotes: Test Set 1: Military and asymmetrical warfare domain,
(ii) Test Set 2: Biology domain, and (iii) Test Set 3: Others (e.g., commonsense queries)
we restricted the cutoff time of each query to 5 minutes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors report that the experimental data was collected on a 4-core 3.40 GHz Intel processor with 32 GB of RAM, and that 18,383 decision trees and the ten best features from subset selection were used.
quotes: The experimental data was collected on a 4-core 3.40 GHz Intel processor with 32 GB of RAM.
We used 18,383 decision trees, and ten best features identified by subset selection in these experiments.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors state that they excluded simple queries answerable without backchaining in a few milliseconds, focused on queries needing several transformations, and drew problems from real-world applications; they report that some benchmark queries initially could not be answered in 20 minutes.
quotes: we excluded simple queries that can be answered without any backchaining in a few milliseconds
this work focused on problems from real-world applications.
Initially some of the queries in our test set could not be answered in 20 minutes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own benchmark scope in Section 6 and footnote 9.

assertions.value: The authors state that the net node score in the experiments is a weighted sum of a score from other heuristics and the decision tree and statistical learning scores, and that the baseline sets both learned-model weights to zero while the DT and SL rows each zero one weight.
quotes: the net score of a node can be written as f(s) = w0+ w1.fDT(s)+ w2.fSL(s).
By setting w2 to 0, we can assess the efficacy of decision tree heuristics
we can study the utility of statistical learning models by setting w1 to 0
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental design in Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Cyc KB has 21.7 million assertions and 652,037 individuals.
quotes: The KB has 21.7 million assertions and 652,037 individuals.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the size of the system it studies; a snapshot as of the paper's date.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in default inference mode, Cyc backward inference uses 21,743 role inclusion axioms, 2,601 inverse role axioms, 365,593 concepts with 986,965 concept inclusion axioms, 817 transitive roles, 99,238 complex role inclusion axioms, and 31,897 binary roles plus 7,980 roles with arities greater than two.
quotes: 21,743 role inclusion axioms
2,601 inverse role axioms
365,593 concepts and 986,965 concept inclusion axioms
817 transitive roles
99,238 complex role inclusion axioms
31,897 binary roles and 7,980 roles with arities greater than two
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the size of the system it studies; a snapshot as of the paper's date.

assertions.value: The authors state that the query (genls ?x Person) has more than 6,700 answers because the predicate genls allows transitive inference in its first argument position.
quotes: The query (genls ?x Person) has more than 6,700 answers
because the predicate ‘genls’ allows transitive inference in its first argument position.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single example count stated without a run description.

assertions.value: The authors define a heuristic module in Cyc as a pair of a weight and a function that assesses the quality of a node, and state that the node with the highest net weighted score is selected for further expansion.
quotes: A heuristic module is a tuple hi = (wi, fi)
wi is the weight of hi.
the node with the highest score is selected for further expansion.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the term where it first uses it, in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that implausible search paths arise when the query does not match the implied context in which an axiom is likely to work.
quotes: Implausible search paths arise when a mismatch exists between the query and the implied context in which an axiom is likely to work.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim motivating the method, argued from two example rules rather than measured.

assertions.value: The authors define a restriction condition as a pair of a variable and a concept, and state that a substitution satisfies it if it maps the variable to a ground term that the sentence set entails to be an instance of the concept.
quotes: Formally, a restriction condition is a pair, x:τ, where x is a variable and τ is a concept.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the term in Section 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that restriction constraints, derived from the results of successful uses of a rule, are represented as decision trees over concept membership, and that a tree for a rule is induced from a training set of successful bindings found by querying the rule's antecedent for a fixed duration of time.
quotes: decision trees are a natural representation for such constraints.
They derive from the results of successful uses of the given rule.
The training set is generated by querying the antecedent of the
rule for a fixed duration of time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how it builds the trees in Section 4 and Figure 1.

assertions.value: The authors describe the CreateTree algorithm: it chooses the most specific maximally covering generalization as the branching test, explores constraints for other variables on the branch where a tuple satisfies the test, considers other values for the variable on the other branch, and stops growing the tree when the number of unexplained training examples is less than a pre-determined fraction of the full training set.
quotes: most specific maximally covering generalization is chosen as
the branching test.
We stop growing the tree (step 2) when the
number of unexplained training examples is less than a
pre-determined fraction of the full training set.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own algorithm in Section 4 and Figure 1.

assertions.value: The authors cite Kent and Hirschberg (1996) for the complexity of top-down decision tree induction being O of m squared times n (printed in the text layer as O(m2.n)), where m is the number of attributes and n is the size of the training set.
quotes: The complexity of top-down decision tree induction is O(m2.n)
m is the number of attributes, and n is the size of the training set [Kent and Hirschberg 1996].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report that the compact decision tree for rule 2 (the objectFoundInLocation rule written as Rule A2) was induced from 1900 bindings and constrains the three variables to GeopoliticalEntity, GeographicalRegion and TerrestrialFunctioningObject.
quotes: The compact decision tree (induced from 1900 bindings) for rule 2
?ARG2:GeopoliticalEntity
?OTHER:GeographicalRegion
?ARG1:TerrestrialFunctioningObject
assertions.certainty_reason: A single worked example from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the decision tree heuristic module prioritizes search paths that satisfy the restriction conditions, so the path using rule A2 for the query (objectFoundInLocation ?x MesophyllCell-001) would be expanded late because MesophyllCell-001 is not transitively a GeographicalRegion.
quotes: This module will prioritize search paths that satisfy the restriction conditions.
would be expanded late because MesophyllCell-001 is not transitively a GeographicalRegion
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative example stated without a measurement on that query.

assertions.value: The authors state that the knowledge base might have thousands of rules relevant for a query, so decision trees alone are not enough and other ways to steer the search toward more productive states are needed.
quotes: since the KB might have thousands of rules that are relevant for a query, we also need other ways to steer the search toward more productive states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit of the decision tree heuristic in Section 4.

assertions.value: The authors report that they ran stored Cyc queries, sampled forty percent of the nodes of the resulting search space, recorded the values of 46 features, and obtained 2.5 million data points.
quotes: Forty percent of the nodes from the resulting space were sampled
the values of the 46 features shown in Figure 2 were recorded. This produced 2.5 million data points.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data collection in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of answers is the performance measure, that predictor variables were z-score normalized, and that, given the extreme variability in the number of answers, they predict log10(1+ number of answers).
quotes: Recall that the number of answers is the performance measure
We performed z-score normalization of the predictor variables
we predict log10(1+ number of answers)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own modeling setup in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that in initial unpublished work, classification techniques such as naive Bayes and logistic regression were tried to predict the likelihood of success of a node, the results were not very encouraging, and they switched to multiple linear regression.
quotes: we experimented with classification techniques
Since the results were not very encouraging, we switched to multiple linear regression.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unpublished result reported without data.
assertions.reader_inference: No numbers are given for the classification attempts, so the claim cannot be checked from this paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that the linear regression model, fit by minimizing root mean squared error in R, was validated by repeated random sub-sampling (90 percent training, repeated 50 times) and 10fold (as printed in the text layer) cross validation, giving mean RMSE of 0.47 and 0.76 respectively.
quotes: The values of wi are determined by minimizing the metric root mean squared error (RMSE).
While using the former method, 90% of the data was selected at random for
training and the rest were used as the test set. This process was repeated 50 times.
The mean RMSE from the two validation methods was 0.47 and 0.76 respectively.
We used the repeated random sub-sampling approach and 10fold cross validation to validate our model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The text names repeated random sub-sampling first and 10-fold cross validation second, so the 0.47 and 0.76 map to them in that order; the RMSE is on the log10(1+ answers) scale, as the target was log-transformed.

assertions.value: The authors report that multiple R squared and adjusted R squared for the model were both 0.76, and an F-statistic printed in the text layer as 1.8*105 (read as 1.8 times ten to the fifth).
quotes: Multiple R2 and adjusted R2 for this model were equal to 0.76, and the F-statistic was 1.8*105.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that exhaustive subset selection identified the best 10 features, and that subset models with these 10 features converged to the R squared of models with all inputs; forward and backward selection gave very similar selections.
quotes: The set of best 10 features as identified by an exhaustive subset selection method is shown in bold in Figure 2.
The R2 value of subset models with these 10 features converged to that of models with all inputs.
All three methods lead to very similar set of selected features.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Which features were selected is shown only in bold in Figure 2, which the text layer does not mark, so the list cannot be recovered from the text.

assertions.value: The authors infer from the selected features that locally available information is insufficient for predicting the complexity of the search space and probing features play an important role, that the search graph needs the right shape and a balance between depth-first and breadth-first search, and that negated literals and disjunctive queries are more difficult to answer.
quotes: Locally available information is insufficient for predicting the complexity of search space, and probing features play an important role in guiding a search.
negated literals and disjunctive queries are more difficult to answer.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's interpretation of the selected feature set.
assertions.reader_inference: Presence of a feature in a best-subset model is correlational evidence, not a test of the causal role the authors describe.

assertions.value: The authors state, from the depth figure, that the conditional probability of success of a node decreases rapidly with depth, and, from the transformation-link figure, that most successful transformation links are added in the initial phase and the utility of adding another drops rapidly.
quotes: We see that the conditional probability of success of a node decreases rapidly with depth.
most of the successful transformation links are added in the initial phase
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, shown in figures.
assertions.reader_inference: Figure 3's axis runs to 0.4; Table 2 (read from the text layer) gives P(success) of 0.940 for one literal and about 0.009 or lower for two or more, a sharp drop with the number of literals.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in contrast to work that selects a small set of relevant axioms, they focus on ordering heuristics that let inference algorithms reason with all axioms, and that to their knowledge no AI work has used decision trees and statistical regression to control inference in large commonsense reasoning systems.
quotes: In contrast, we focus on ordering heuristics that enable inference algorithms to reason with all axioms.
no work in the AI community has used decision trees and statistical regression-based methods to control inference in large commonsense reasoning systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's novelty claim, unverified here.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper cites Taylor et al. 2007 (reinforcement learning to guide Cyc inference), which the authors distinguish from their approach.

assertions.value: The authors state future work: test the heuristics over an even larger set of queries to understand their dynamics, extend the decision tree implementation to make probabilistic assessments, try other statistical models (regression splines, random forests), and couple the approach with a decision-theoretic model.
quotes: First, we need to test
these heuristics over even larger set of queries to understand
Second, we want to extend our decision tree
implementation to make probabilistic assessments.
regression splines, random forests
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own open problems in Section 7.
